title: How to write billing narratives clients accept on Mac: a lawyer's guide for 2026
metaTitle: How to write billing narratives clients accept on Mac (2026)
description: Clients reject vague billing narratives. Write each entry with the task, the matter, the reason and the result, then check it against their rules.

billing narratives for lawyers on Mac
intro: To write a billing narrative clients accept, name the task, the matter, the reason for it, and the result in one plain line. Most rejected narratives fail because they are vague, bundle several tasks together, or describe work the client never agreed to pay for. This page shows how to fix each problem on a Mac, what each rejection costs you, and where a voice assistant helps and where it does not.
tldr: Name the task, the matter, the reason and the result in every entry.
Split bundled entries so each task has its own line and its own time.
Read the client's billing guidelines before you write, not after a rejection.
Review entries the same day, while you still remember the work.
I found no public study that counts rejected narratives, so treat these fixes as good practice, not proven results.

blocks.text: Why clients reject a billing narrative

A client usually rejects a narrative for one of a few reasons. The entry is too vague to judge. The work looks like something the client never asked for. Or the time looks large for the words used. The client's billing reviewer is not reading for style. They are scanning for a reason to cut the line.

Most rejections are about the words, not the work. A capable lawyer can do excellent work and still write 'Attention to matter' on the bill. That line invites a cut, because the reviewer cannot see what happened inside it.

Billing rules matter more than most lawyers expect. Many clients set their own standards for narratives. Those rules can cover length, banned phrases, task codes and which tasks they pay for at all. The rules often sit in an outside counsel guideline or a panel agreement, not in your head.
What a rejected narrative costs you

The first cost is not on the invoice. A rejected entry is time you already spent that will not be paid. Someone then has to find the matter, reopen the line, rewrite it and send it back. That rewrite is often unbilled too.

The second cost is trust. A client who cuts several lines on one invoice reads the next one more slowly. Reviews take longer, and disputes start earlier. Some clients respond by asking for a fixed fee or a budget, which changes how you price the whole matter.

items: Unbilled rewrite time. You spend time on the same entry twice, and the second pass rarely earns a fee.
Slower payment. A disputed line can hold up a whole invoice while both sides argue over it.
Write-downs. The firm removes the line, so the time you recorded never becomes revenue.
Tighter reviews. A reviewer who finds vague lines will check the next invoice more closely.

blocks.text: The numbers I could and could not find

I searched for data on rejected billing narratives and found none. No source I could open counts how often clients reject narratives, or what those rejections cost a firm. Several primary pages returned errors, so I left out their figures.

What exists is context about pressure on billing. Thomson Reuters reported that worked rates rose 7.4% in Q2 2025, while productivity fell 1.3% and demand rose 1.6%. When rates climb, each hour on a bill attracts more scrutiny. That link is my reading, not a finding in the report.

The ABA Journal reported that 65.5% of lawyers and staff in a 2025 ALM/Law.com Compass survey said billable-hour pressure hurts their mental well-being. Pressure can push entries to be written in a rush. The survey did not measure narratives, so test that idea against your own invoices.
How to write a narrative clients accept
Use one line per task. Each line should answer four questions: what you did, on which matter, why it was needed, and what came of it. You do not need long sentences. You need specific words.

items: Start with a task verb. Use drafted, reviewed, called, researched or attended.
Name the document, person or issue. Drop 'work on,' 'attention to' and 'review file.'
Add the reason in one clause. Say why this matter needed the work now.
State the result or next step. Say what now exists, or what happens next.

blocks.caption: Examples are invented to show the pattern. Match them to your matter and your client's rules.
rows: Call with client's in-house counsel on settlement terms
Names the party and the subject
Reviewed discovery responses for gaps before the meet and confer call
Names the item, the check and the purpose
Emailed the client the signed engagement letter for the file
Names the item and why it was sent
Drafted the reply to the opposing motion to dismiss
Names the document and the step

blocks.text: Here is a worked example. Start with 'Review file re: Johnson.' Rewrite it as 'Reviewed the discovery responses for Johnson for gaps before the meet and confer call.' The task, the item and the purpose now show. The client can judge that line without emailing you.
Worked example: splitting a bundled entry

Bundled entries are hard to defend. Take one line that reads 'Research, draft memo, call with client, emails.' The reviewer cannot tell which part was useful or how long each part took. Split it into four lines. Each line gets its own task, its own time and its own reason.
Splitting also protects the rest of the entry. If the client cuts the call, the research and the memo still stand. A bundled line gives the reviewer one easy place to cut everything.

blocks.title: Test your line
blocks.text: Read the entry aloud as if you are the client's billing reviewer. If you cannot tell what was done and why, the reviewer cannot either.
Edge cases that get narratives rejected
Some kinds of work get questioned more than others. Rules differ by client, so read the guideline first. These are the ones that need extra care in the wording.

items: Internal meetings. Name who attended and why the meeting helped this matter.
Travel time. State whether the client agreed to pay for it, and on which matter.
Administrative tasks. Scheduling, copying and filing often fall under overhead. Check before you bill them.
Several people on one task. Say who did what, so the client does not pay twice for one review.
Long entries. A single line that runs for hours invites questions. Split it by task.

blocks.text: Edge cases also include work you did for another matter. Never move time between matters to fit a budget. Correct the entry and tell your billing contact why.
Mistakes people make when they fix narratives

The first mistake is padding. Adding words does not help a vague entry. 'Reviewed documents in detail and considered the issues carefully' says less than the short version. Cut the filler and name the work.
The second mistake is describing work you did not do. A narrative must match the time and the task. If an entry was wrong, correct it and explain the change to your billing contact.
The third mistake is waiting. A rushed rewrite on the day the invoice goes out is more likely to add errors. Review entries each evening while the work is fresh.

blocks.title: Client data and firm rules
blocks.text: Follow your employer's rules on client and matter data. Before you paste a narrative into any AI tool, check whether your firm allows it. If you are unsure, ask your supervisor or your firm's risk or IT team first.
Where Lazur helps, and where it does not

Lazur helps with reading and wording. Hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask about what is on your screen, and Lazur answers out loud. It points at controls, guides you one click at a time, and dictates text at your cursor. You still review every word before it goes to a client.

Next steps

Start with one client and one invoice. Rewrite the entries most likely to be cut. Send the draft to a colleague who did not work on the matter, and ask what each line means. If they cannot say, rewrite it again.
For drafts in Word, see [Word for lawyers on Mac](/for/lawyers/word). For client email, see [Outlook for lawyers on Mac](/for/lawyers/outlook).

faq.question: What does a billing narrative need to say?
faq.answer: A billing narrative should say what task was done, on which matter, why it was needed, and what came of it. Keep it to one task per entry. Your client's guidelines may set a word limit or ban certain phrases, so check them first.

faq.question: Can I reuse the same narrative for similar tasks?
faq.answer: Only when the task and the matter are truly the same. Reused text often names the wrong matter, the wrong party or the wrong document. Change the details each time, even when the work looks alike.

faq.question: Should I bill internal meetings?
faq.answer: It depends on the client's guidelines and your engagement terms. Many clients want internal meetings described with attendees and purpose. Some clients do not pay for them at all. Ask before you bill them to a matter.

faq.question: How do I know if a narrative is too vague?
faq.answer: Ask a colleague who did not work on the matter to read it. If they cannot tell what you did and why, the client will likely ask too. Words like review, work on and attention to are common warning signs.

faq.question: Can Lazur write my billing narratives for me?
faq.answer: Lazur can draft and dictate text, but you must read it and decide what goes on the bill. Lazur only knows what is on your screen or what you tell it. Check every line before it goes to a client.

faq.question: Does Lazur send my client data anywhere?
faq.answer: Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Follow your firm's rules on client data before you use it on matters.

faq.question: Is there a way to do this without any paid tool?
faq.answer: Yes. Use the four-part line, read each client's guidelines once, and keep a note per client in Apple Notes. Turn on Dictation in System Settings > Keyboard > Dictation, and use Word's Find (⌘F) to search drafts for vague phrases.

costs.title: Time you already spent goes unpaid
costs.text: A rejected entry is work you did and cannot bill. Then you spend more time finding the matter, reopening the line and rewriting it. That rewrite is often not billable either, so the cost lands on your own hours.

costs.title: Payment slows on disputed invoices
costs.text: A disputed line can hold up a whole invoice. Both sides go back and forth on one entry while the rest of the bill waits. The firm carries the cost of that delay until the dispute resolves.

costs.title: Lines cut from the bill
costs.text: A write-down removes time from the bill. The time you recorded never becomes revenue, even though you did the work. Repeated cuts on one client make the matter harder to justify.

costs.title: Tighter reviews and fixed fees
costs.text: A client who finds vague lines reads the next invoice line by line. Reviews get longer. Some clients respond by asking for fixed fees or budgets, which changes how you price future work.

causes.title: Entries written at the end of the week
causes.text: Memory fades fast. At the end of a long week, a task blurs into a general label such as review file or attention to matter. Writing the narrative the same day keeps the detail the client needs to judge it.

causes.title: Several tasks bundled into one line
causes.text: Bundling feels quick when you enter time. But a reviewer cannot tell which task took the time, or whether each one belongs on the bill. A bundled line gives the reviewer one place to cut everything.

causes.title: Templates copied from older matters
causes.text: A narrative reused from another matter can name the wrong party, the wrong document or the wrong step in the case. Clients spot these mismatches quickly, and then they doubt the rest of the invoice.

causes.title: Client guidelines nobody read
causes.text: Outside counsel guidelines can set word limits, banned phrases, task codes and which tasks get paid at all. Lawyers often learn these rules only after a rejection. Reading the guideline once, and keeping a short note, prevents most repeat cuts.

causes.title: Pressure on billable hours
causes.text: The ABA Journal reported that 65.5% of lawyers and staff in a 2025 survey said billable-hour pressure hurts their mental well-being. Under that pressure, entries can get shorter and less specific. This is a plausible link, not one I could measure for narratives.

causes.title: Describing the outcome instead of the task
causes.text: Entries like successful call with client describe how it went, not what you did. The client wants to see the work. Name the task first, then the result, so the reviewer sees the effort behind the line.

causes.title: Narratives written for yourself
causes.text: Shorthand that makes sense to you can mean nothing to the client. Initials, internal matter nicknames and private abbreviations confuse reviewers. Write each narrative as if the client's billing team will read it, because they will.

fixes.title: Use the four-part line on every entry
fixes.text: Every narrative should answer four questions: what task, on which matter, why it was needed, and what it produced. Keep the line to one task. Read it back once, out loud, before you save it.

fixes.title: Split bundled entries before you save
fixes.text: If one line holds research, a draft and a call, enter separate lines. Each line should have its own time and its own task. Splitting takes a little extra typing and protects the rest of the entry if the client cuts one part.

fixes.title: Keep a one-page guideline note per client
fixes.text: Open each active client's billing guideline once. Copy the rules that matter into a note in Apple Notes or Word. Include word limits, banned phrases, task codes and tasks the client will not pay. Keep the note open while you write.

fixes.title: Review entries each evening
fixes.text: Set a short review each evening. Read each narrative against the four parts. Fix vague lines while the work is still fresh. Daily review is far easier than a rushed rewrite the week an invoice goes out.

fixes.title: Dictate the narrative as the task ends
fixes.text: Turn on Dictation in System Settings > Keyboard > Dictation. Then speak the four-part line as soon as you finish the task. Read the text back before you save it, since speech tools can mishear names and legal terms.

fixes.title: Search your draft for vague phrases
fixes.text: Paste draft narratives into a Word document, then press ⌘F and search for phrases such as review file, work on, attention to and emails re. Each hit is a line to rewrite. The search takes seconds for each invoice.

fixes.title: Compare the draft with the invoice before sending
fixes.text: If the invoice changed after the draft, open both versions in Word and use Review > Compare to see what changed. Check that every narrative still matches its amount. A quiet change to one line can undo a careful rewrite.

fixes.title: Log every rejection and the reason
fixes.text: Keep a short list of rejected lines and the reason the client gave. Note the client, the task type and the wording. After a few invoices, patterns appear, such as one phrase that keeps getting cut.

fixes.title: Ask the client what a narrative must show
fixes.text: If a client keeps cutting one task type, email the billing contact and ask what they need to see. Ask one specific question, such as whether they want attendees named for internal meetings. Save the answer in your guideline note.

plan.label: Monday
plan.title: Collect the guidelines
plan.text: Open the billing guideline for each active client. Copy the rules that affect narratives into one note per client in Apple Notes. Include word limits, banned phrases and tasks the client will not pay.

plan.label: Daily
plan.title: Write the four-part line
plan.text: Write each narrative the day you do the task. Use one task per line. Read it once, out loud, before you save it. If you dictate, check the text for misheard names and terms.

plan.label: Evening
plan.title: Run a short end-of-day review
plan.text: Read each narrative from that day against the four parts. Fix any line that says only review, work on or attention to. Move on once every line names a task and a reason.

plan.label: Wednesday
plan.title: Split bundled lines
plan.text: Find any entry that holds more than one task. Split it into separate lines, each with its own time. Check that each new line has a clear reason. Keep the total time the same as before.

plan.label: Thursday
plan.title: Search the draft invoice
plan.text: Paste the draft narratives into a Word document. Press ⌘F and search for vague phrases. Rewrite every hit. If the invoice changed after the first draft, use Review > Compare to check the differences.

plan.label: Friday
plan.title: Send one question
plan.text: Email the client's billing contact about any task type that keeps getting cut. Ask one specific question. Save the answer in the guideline note so the next invoice reflects it.

plan.label: Monday after
plan.title: Log what came back
plan.text: Read the client's reply on the last invoice. Note which lines were cut, which were accepted and why. Use that list to change how you write the next week of entries.
